docs.title: Groundline
docs.text:
Grounded context infrastructure for engineering teams.

Your team’s memory, in git—searchable on your machine.

Groundline is a template repository: durable knowledge lives as reviewed Markdown under knowledge/, changes flow through Pull Requests, and an optional local retrieval service grounds assistants and humans in what the team merged—with citations, not chat memory.

docs.title: Groundline — Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Draft (aligned with REQUIREMENTS.md) Owner: GYANESH Last updated: 2025-11-06

This document describes the logical and physical architecture of Groundline: a git-hosted corpus of Markdown, a local RAG index and services, and assistant-agnostic clients (HTTP, MCP, CLI). Normative behaviour, schemas, and phases remain in REQUIREMENTS; this file is the systems view for implementers and reviewers.

docs.title: 1. Goals and constraints
docs.text:
Goal How the architecture supports it Single source of truth Markdown + YAML front matter in git; PR merges only (REQUIREMENTS §4). Compounding knowledge Full corpus at a commit SHA drives the index; each merge extends coverage (§1, §3). Grounded agent use Retrieve → mandatory rerank → context packs → citations on any generation path (§5.5–§5.7, §5.10). No vendor lock-in Canonical REST + JSON on loopback; optional MCP mirroring the same operations (§5.9, §5.12). Local-first Index and models run on the developer machine by default; optional CI validates corpus (§5.2, §7–§8, §12).

Non-goals for architecture v1: Mandatory cloud embedding, proprietary-only IDE APIs, or storing work-tracker exports in the corpus (§3).

docs.title: 2. System context (C4-style)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph contributors [Contributors]
    Dev[Developers / QE / PM / DM]
  end

  subgraph git_host [Git host]
    Repo[(Groundline repo)]
  end

  subgraph local [Contributor machine]
    Corpus[knowledge/*.md + meta]
    Pipeline[Index pipeline]
    Store[(Vector + optional sparse index)]
    API[Local HTTP API]
    MCP[MCP stdio python -m ki mcp]
    Manifest[.rag manifest gitignored]
  end

  subgraph clients [Clients]
    IDE[IDE assistants]
    Term[Terminal / scripts]
  end

  Dev -->|PR merge| Repo
  Dev -->|clone / pull| Corpus
  Corpus --> Pipeline
  Pipeline --> Store
  Pipeline --> Manifest
  API --> Store
  MCP -->|HTTP tools| API
  IDE -->|localhost REST| API
  IDE -->|MCP host| MCP
  Term -->|curl / CLI| API
  Repo -->|same files| Corpus

Responsibility split:

  • Git remote: Version history, review, branch protection — not the runtime for retrieval.
  • Local runtime: Build index from working tree or pinned commit, serve queries with health (index_status, sync_status) (§5.6, §12.1–§12.2).

docs.title: 3. Repository layout (information architecture)
docs.text:
High-level map (§6):

knowledge/
  technical/      # architecture, runbooks, ADRs
  delivery/       # curated delivery summaries, analysis
  testing/        # QE-led quality knowledge
  functional/     # product / glossary / features
  meta/           # golden queries, policies, templates (paths may vary)
scripts/          # indexer, API server, validators (when implemented)
meta/             # contribution templates, author-profile.example.yaml, etc.
.rag/             # generated index + manifest (gitignored)

Front matter carries title, area, type, status, author_role, and domain derived from path or validated against it (§6.1 Domain inference).

docs.title: 4. Logical components
docs.text: Component Responsibility Corpus Authoritative Markdown under knowledge/; evolves by PR. Ingest Discover files, parse front matter, normalize body. Chunker Structure-aware splits; stable chunk ids; metadata propagation (§5.4). Embedder (MVP) tf‑idf word vectors per chunk (dense surrogate until neural embeddings); model id in manifest. Sparse index (MVP) Okapi BM25 over chunk term frequencies — hybrid with dense, fused via RRF (§5.5, §5.11). Retriever First stage: hybrid RRF → candidate set (e.g. top 20–40). Reranker Mandatory second stage; local cross-encoder or light ranker (§5.5). Context assembler Caps per doc, related: expansion, inclusion_reason, optional diversification (§5.10). API REST JSON: retrieve, context_pack, health, optional get_chunk / neighbours (§5.6). MCP adapter Optional stdio server (python3 -m ki mcp after pip install -e ".[mcp]"): tools teamkm_* call the same local HTTP API; agent loop stays in the host (§5.9, §5.12; MCP.md). Validator scripts/validate_frontmatter.py: schema + path/domain rules (§6.1, §8). Sync (optional) Fetch + fast-forward only when safe; feeds staleness for reindex (§12.2).

docs.title: 5. Index build data flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  A[knowledge/**/*.md] --> B[Parse front matter]
  B --> C[Strip / attach doc metadata to chunks]
  C --> D[Structure-aware chunking]
  D --> E[tf-idf vectors per chunk]
  D --> F[BM25 stats per chunk]
  E --> G[.rag/index.staging]
  F --> G
  G --> H[Atomic rename to .rag/index]
  H --> I[manifest.json after success]

Incremental build: Content-hash per file; re-chunk/re-embed only changed files (§5.5). Fingerprint: Align index staleness with git tree / hashes (§12.1).

docs.title: 6. Query / context-pack data flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Client as Client (IDE / script)
  participant API as Local API
  participant R as Retriever
  participant RR as Reranker
  participant A as Context assembler

  Client->>API: query + optional filters (area, domain, profile)
  API->>R: hybrid or dense (phase-dependent)
  R-->>API: candidates N
  API->>RR: query + passages
  RR-->>API: scored reorder
  API->>A: top passages + limits
  A-->>API: context pack (grouped, inclusion_reason)
  API-->>Client: JSON + citations

Contract: Responses expose paths, line ranges, retrieval and rerank scores where applicable (§5.6). Downstream generation must cite chunks or mark gaps (§5.7).

docs.title: Index freshness and golden eval (implemented)
docs.text:
Surface Role python3 -m ki --root . status CLI report: manifest corpus_fingerprint vs live corpus hash GET /v1/health index_stale, index_stale_now, corpus_fingerprint_current / _indexed python3 -m ki --root . eval Golden queries: recall@k + MRR@k (meta/golden_queries.yaml) python3 scripts/golden_queries.py Same harness as ki eval (CI uses this entrypoint)

Re-index when stale: python3 -m ki --root . index. See TESTING.md.

docs.title: 7. Contribution flow (retrieval-first)
docs.text:
Designed so agents do not invent duplicates blindly (§5.8):

  1. Refresh index to merge base.
  2. Retrieve similar chunks for draft outline or title.
  3. Present top‑k with scores and paths.
  4. Recommend edit existing vs new file under knowledge/<domain>/....
  5. Human opens PR; CI validates front matter and optionally runs golden-query regression (§8).

Optional: contribute --dry-run or PR bot listing related docs (§5.8, §10).

docs.title: 8. Session lifecycle (developer experience)
docs.text:
Primary trigger: coding-assistant session starts MCP or local API → background sync (if enabled) → index if missing/stale (§12.1).

  • Git hooks are supplementary; they do not run on server-side clone (§12.1 caveat).
  • Auto-sync: Fast-forward only when working tree is clean; block on dirty/diverged (§12.2).

docs.title: 9. Security and compliance (architecture-relevant)
docs.text: Topic Approach Secrets / PII Out of corpus; pre-merge checks recommended (§3, §7). Network Default loopback binding; optional LAN with documented risk (§5.9). Model policy Embedding/reranker documented in meta/; air-gap teams use local models (§5.3, §7). Audit Citations + inclusion reasons for traceability (§5.7, §5.10).

docs.title: 10. Phase alignment (build order)
docs.text: Phase Architecture emphasis MVP Dense index, mandatory rerank, context packs with caps + related, citations, HTTP + optional MCP, health + fingerprint (§10). V1+ Hybrid retrieval, MMMR/hardening, richer expansion, OpenAPI (§5.11, §10). V2 Optional PR bot, published index artefacts (§10).

docs.title: 11. Open implementation choices
docs.text: Tracked in REQUIREMENTS §9: vector store, embedding/reranker models, chunk defaults, API port/versioning, hook vs MCP-only automation, etc.

docs.title: Protecting main on GitHub
docs.text: GitHub shows “Your main branch isn’t protected” when main has no rule that blocks force-push/deletion or enforces checks before merge.

docs.title: Why automation may fail from the CLI
docs.text:
The REST API for classic branch protection can return HTTP 403 for private repositories on a free personal account with a message like:

Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public to enable this feature.

That does not mean branch protection is impossible—it means API-based configuration may be blocked until you upgrade, move the repo to an organization with the right plan, or change visibility (if policy allows).

docs.title: Fix via the UI (recommended when the banner appears)
docs.text:
1. Open the repo on GitHub → Settings → Branches (or use Protect this branch in the banner).
  2. Add branch protection rule for main.
  3. Enable (aligned with Contributing):
  4. Require a pull request before merging
  5. Require approvals: at least 1 (tune per team)
  6. Require status checks to pass (our workflow job is named test in .github/workflows/ci.yml)
  7. Require conversation resolution before merging (optional but useful)
  8. Do not allow bypassing the above settings (admins follow rules too), if available
  9. Save.

After the next push to main or a PR run, the check test will appear in the dropdown for required checks.

docs.title: Required check name
docs.text: The CI workflow defines a single job test (see ci.yml). In branch protection, pick test as the required check.

docs.title: Alternatives if your plan blocks protection
docs.text:
• GitHub Pro / Team / Enterprise — enables full branch protection on private repos.
  • Organization repo — often matches team policies better than a personal fork.
  • Process-only — keep merging only via PR and never git push --force to main (weak without server-side enforcement).

docs.title: How to use Groundline (simple guide)
docs.text:
Audience: Anyone on the team—you do not need to be a programmer to help with the knowledge in this repo. Technical setup is optional; writing and reviewing clear notes is the main job.

Deep detail: REQUIREMENTS.md • Developers: Contributing • Leaders: LEADERSHIP_PITCH.md

docs.title: 1. What Groundline is (in plain words)
docs.text:
Think of Groundline as a shared notebook in git:

  • Important things the team agrees on live in Markdown files under knowledge/ (not lost in chat or tickets).
  • Changes go through a Pull Request (PR) so someone reviews before it becomes official on main.
  • Optional: after install, a small program can search those notes and hand relevant passages to humans or AI tools so answers stay grounded in what the team actually merged.

docs.title: 2. What “good” looks like (for non-techies)
docs.text:
You do Why it helps Write short, factual notes when something important is decided or learned The next person (or AI) can find it instead of guessing Put files in the right area (technical, delivery, testing, functional, meta) Keeps topics grouped so search stays useful Use draft in the front matter until the PR is merged; the system can mark docs reviewed after merge Shows what is still in progress vs officially part of the corpus Ask for a reviewer who knows the topic Catches mistakes early

You do not have to run Python, servers, or AI tools to contribute text—that can be done in GitHub’s web editor or with help from a developer.

docs.title: 3. The team process (five steps)
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  A[1. Write or edit a markdown file under knowledge/] --> B[2. Open a Pull Request]
  B --> C[3. Teammate reviews]
  C --> D[4. Merge to main]
  D --> E[5. Optional: rebuild search index locally]
  1. Write — Add or change a .md file under the right knowledge/... folder. A small template sits at the top of each file (called front matter): title, area, status, etc.
  2. Pull Request — Propose the change so others can see a diff and comment.
  3. Review — At least one person checks facts, tone, and placement.
  4. Merge — When merged to main, the note is part of the official corpus (and automation may set reviewed on drafts—see Contributing).
  5. Search (optional) — People who installed the tooling can refresh the index and ask questions against merged notes—always citing which file the answer came from.

docs.title: 4. Roles at a glance
docs.text:
Role Typical focus PM / DM Product intent, scope, acceptance-style summaries under functional/ or delivery/ Developers How things are built, trade-offs, runbooks under technical/ QE / testing How we validate, risks, regressions under testing/ Anyone Small meta/ notes about how we use this repo are fine if they help the team

If unsure where a note goes, open a PR anyway and ask in the description—a reviewer can suggest a better path.

docs.title: 5. If you use an AI coding assistant
docs.text:
Idea: Let the assistant read Groundline first, then answer or edit code—so it uses your merged notes, not only generic training data.

  • Simple path: Paste relevant excerpts from knowledge/ into the chat (still cite the file path in your question).
  • Team setup (technical): Someone runs the local API and optionally connects MCP so the assistant can call search tools automatically—see MCP.md and the documentation home / README on GitHub.

Rule of thumb: Prefer retrieve → then act (search notes first, then change code or docs).

docs.title: 6. Words you might hear
docs.text: Term Simple meaning Corpus All the approved markdown under knowledge/ PR / Pull Request A proposed change others review before merge main The default branch—what counts as “current official” for the team Front matter The small YAML block at the top of a file with title, status, tags Index / RAG A built search layer over the corpus (optional for authors; useful for power users) MCP A standard way for editors to talk to small helper programs (optional)

docs.title: Groundline — Leadership brief
docs.text: Audience: Engineering leadership, product leadership, delivery management Companion: ARCHITECTURE.md (how it works), REQUIREMENTS.md (full spec) Last updated: 2025-11-06

docs.title: Elevator statement
docs.text: Groundline is a team-owned knowledge base where durable know-how lives in git as Markdown, and a local retrieval service makes that corpus queryable by any coding assistant—with mandatory reranking, structured context packs, and citations so answers are grounded in what the team actually merged, not in model memory alone.

docs.title: The problem we are solving
docs.text:
• When people leave or rotate, undocumented context walks out the door; handovers and ramp-up stay expensive.
  • Chat and tickets do not compound: they scatter and age; they are poor as a single source of truth.
  • AI coding tools without retrieval reuse generic patterns and can hallucinate on your stack, your history, and your quality bar.

This product does not replace good management or mentorship. It institutionalizes what the team agrees to write, review, and merge—and makes that corpus easy to use during real engineering work.

docs.title: What we are offering (product)
docs.text: Layer What it is Corpus Markdown under knowledge/ with YAML metadata; PR-only merges (REQUIREMENTS §4). Intelligence Local RAG: chunk → embed → retrieve → mandatory rerank → context packs (not naive “top‑k cosine” only) (§5.4–§5.6, §5.10, §5.11). Access HTTP on localhost (canonical) plus optional MCP stdio server (python3 -m ki mcp, tools teamkm_*) so Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot-class tools, or scripts integrate the same way—the host runs the agent loop (§5.9, §5.12). Adoption Any team can treat this repo as a template: clone, point origin at their remote, customize layout and policy (§4.5).

docs.title: Features leadership should care about
docs.text:
1. Git as source of truth — Diff, review, history, and compliance are the same as for code; no second silo to fund separately.
  2. Cross-role coverage — Room for technical, delivery, testing (QE), and functional (PM) knowledge linked by area and metadata (§2–§3, §6).
  3. Grounded AI assistance — Default path is retrieve then analyze with citations; unsupported claims are explicit gaps, not silent invention (§5.7).
  4. Quality-oriented retrieval — Mandatory rerank plus context assembly (caps, related expansion, inclusion reasons) improves what actually reaches the model (§5.5, §5.10).
  5. Assistant-agnostic — You are not betting the strategy on one IDE vendor (§5.12).
  6. Measurable quality over time — Golden query sets and recall targets push tuning from opinion to data (§5.5, §7, §11).
  7. Conflict and deprecation rules — Stale or contradictory docs are handled in the open, not blended silently at retrieval time (§4.4, §5.10).

docs.title: Outcomes (what success looks like)
docs.text:
Outcome Indicators Faster, safer delivery Less time re-discovering prior decisions, failure modes, and test lore; agents reference your corpus before changing code. Shorter ramp-up New hires and transfers find reviewed narratives by area (engineering, QE, product) instead of only tribal knowledge. Stronger handovers Knowledge is in-repo and versioned; what was merged is discoverable with provenance. Compounding returns Each merged PR widens retrieval coverage; the index at main reflects cumulative learning (§1, §11). Lower vendor risk Integration through standard HTTP/MCP avoids single-tool dependency for the knowledge layer (§5.12).

These outcomes scale with discipline: teams that merge curated updates regularly and use retrieval in the loop see the largest benefit. A repo that is empty or stale behaves like one—no architecture fixes that.

docs.title: Success metrics (starter set)
docs.text:
Aligned with REQUIREMENTS §11:

docs.text:

Does not replace: Headcount judgment, architecture ownership, security review, or product prioritization.

Does reduce: Repeated rediscovery, contradictory one-off docs in chat, and ungrounded AI answers when the answer was already in the corpus.

docs.title: Groundline — Requirements
docs.text:
Project name: Groundline (repository / product name for this RAG knowledge base). Status: Draft for review Owner: GYANESH Last updated: 2025-11-06

This document captures the planned behaviour of Groundline: a git-hosted, RAG-based knowledge base for agent-assisted development. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the core pattern: knowledge lives in the repo as normal files; a local pipeline chunks, embeds, and indexes them so agents retrieve grounded passages before (or instead of) answering. The retrieval service runs locally (e.g. localhost); any agent coding assistant that can call HTTP or MCP can integrate—assistant-agnostic by design (§5.12). Cursor, Claude, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, or a shell script are examples, not hard dependencies. Revise sections as the team agrees.

Core product idea: Knowledge compounds. Every merged contribution adds to a shared corpus. Over weeks and months the index reflects technical, delivery, testing, and product learning—so developers, QE, PMs, and the dev manager can pull the same grounded context when improving products and features they own (new builds, refactors, quality hardening, roadmap decisions), instead of re-deriving it from memory or chat.

What this product is for (any team): Maintain durable, reviewable knowledge in git; share it across roles via a single corpus; reuse prior decisions, analysis, and testing lore instead of rediscovering them; support analysis (human and agent) with retrieval that grounds answers in cited chunks rather than model recall alone. This repository is intended as a reusable template: a team clones it (or uses it as a GitHub template / fork), creates their own remote where they push markdown under knowledge/ and evolve meta/, skills, and tooling to match policy—see §4.5.

See also: ARCHITECTURE.md (systems view, data flows) — LEADERSHIP_PITCH.md (executive brief: value, outcomes, adoption) — TESTING.md (tests and corruption guardrails).

docs.title: 1. Purpose and problem
docs.text:
Teams doing agentic development produce many markdown (and related) documents: decisions, runbooks, API notes, domain language, and experiment logs. That knowledge is fragmented and hard to reuse as trusted context for tools like Cursor or Claude.

Goal: A single version-controlled project that is easy to maintain and extend: contributors commit markdown (and similar) like any other repo work; after merge, they (or CI) rebuild the RAG index with simple commands. The system stays accurate by tying assistant outputs to retrieved chunks with citations, not to model recall alone.

Cumulative value: Each PR adds or updates durable notes; the RAG index is rebuilt from the full corpus at a given commit. The whole history of contributions is what makes retrieval better over time—coverage of edge cases, test lore, product intent, and operational reality deepens as the team commits.

docs.title: 2. Stakeholders
docs.text: Role Count Responsibility (high level) Developers 8 Commit completed work and analysis tied to delivery (implementation notes, trade-offs, integration points, follow-ups); review peers’ PRs; use retrieval when building or maintaining features QE 1 Commit testing knowledge: test plans, charters, regression notes, defect patterns, environment/setup gotchas, quality risks; use retrieval for regression and quality planning Dev Manager 1 Governance, access, escalation; use retrieval for cross-team alignment and risk on areas the team supports Product Manager 1 Author/approve functional product knowledge; align functional docs with product themes; use retrieval to ground feature specs and decisions in prior engineering and QE context

docs.title: 3.1 Domains
docs.text:
• Technical: Architecture, ADRs, conventions, libraries, deployment, debugging notes, integration contracts, performance, security considerations.
  • Delivery / engineering narrative: Summaries of work completed, analysis, and discussion outcomes from the team’s delivery work (feature, fix, spike, etc.). Curated only—no dump of raw chat or external ticket threads. External work trackers are out of scope for this repo: do not store keys, links, or exports from tools such as JIRA; capture only what belongs in this knowledge base as standalone prose.
  • Functional / product: Features, user journeys, glossary, business rules, acceptance criteria summaries (not a full backlog replacement).
  • Testing / quality (QE-owned primary author): Test strategy excerpts, coverage notes, automation hooks, known flakiness, sign-off context suitable for reuse by dev and PM readers.

docs.title: 3.2 Primary formats (initial)
docs.text:
• Markdown (.md) as the default interchange.
  • Optional later: diagrams (Mermaid in-repo), structured YAML/JSON for machine-readable facts.

docs.title: 3.3 Contribution rhythm (expected behaviour)
docs.text:
• Developers add or update knowledge when a unit of work reaches a sensible checkpoint (e.g. done, or end of a spike): what shipped, what was decided, what to watch in maintenance.
  • QE adds or updates knowledge when test phases complete or when durable testing assets deserve a canonical home in the repo (still merged via PR).
  • Over time, cumulative commits improve the local index: newcomers and agents query prior episodes for the same subsystem, feature area, or defect class.
  • Cross-role context: The same retrieval interface supports dev (how we built it), QE (how we broke it / verified it), PM (what we intended for the product), DM (themes and risks)—so feature and maintenance work stays aligned with recorded intent and reality.

Out of scope (v1): Storing secrets, credentials, or PII. Those must never be committed. Work-tracker payloads (e.g. ticket keys, ticket URLs, or copy-pasted threads from JIRA or similar systems) are not part of this knowledge base—keep that tooling outside the repo; here we keep self-contained knowledge only. If the team later needs traceability, decide a separate policy (e.g. opaque internal refs); do not block MVP on it.

docs.title: 3.4 RAG and “easy to maintain”
docs.text:
Maintenance should feel like ordinary documentation practice, not a separate product:

  • Source of truth = files in git. No proprietary silo; diff, review, and history are standard.
  • Contributing = add or edit markdown under knowledge/, open a PR, get approval, merge.
  • Indexing = automated or one command after pull/merge (e.g. “rebuild RAG index”), with incremental rebuild where possible so daily work stays fast.
  • Chunking and embeddings are implementation details documented in meta/ so the team can tune them without rewriting prose.

docs.title: 4.1 Git as source of truth
docs.text:
• All knowledge lives in a dedicated git repository (monorepo for knowledge only, or a clearly named subtree if nested).
  • No direct pushes to the default branch (e.g. main): changes land only via Pull Request (PR).
  • PRs are the approval gate: at least one reviewer (policy TBD: e.g. one peer + optional domain owner).

docs.title: 4.2 What may be merged (merge criteria — draft)
docs.text:
Reviewers check that contributions:

  1. Belong in the knowledge base (not transient chat dumps without curation).
  2. Are accurate and, where possible, cite sources (doc link, code path, commit date, or other references that live inside this repo or your public/private docs—not external ticket IDs unless the team explicitly allows a separate policy later).
  3. Follow the repository layout and naming (see §6).
  4. Avoid secrets, unreleasable data, and speculative statements presented as fact (mark uncertainty explicitly, e.g. “Open question: …”).
  5. Include front matter per §6.1 (validated in CI).
  6. Distinguish roles: developer commits should read as engineering/delivery knowledge; QE commits as testing/quality knowledge—cross-link when the same feature or area spans both.

docs.title: 4.3 Branch protection (recommended)
docs.text:
• Require PR reviews before merge.
  • Optional: required status checks (e.g. lint, link check, index build in CI).
  • Optional: CODEOWNERS by area (e.g. functional/ → PM + delegate).

docs.title: 4.4 Conflicting or superseded knowledge
docs.text:
When retrieval surfaces two passages that disagree for the same scope (product version, environment, or “current default”):

  1. Do not silently merge contradictory facts in prose; reviewers resolve in a follow-up PR.
  2. Historical knowledge must remain valid where it still applies (older stacks, older product lines). Prefer status: legacy_reviewed plus applies_to / doc_version (see §6.1) so agents and humans retrieve version-scoped truth instead of deleting old notes.
  3. Reserve status: deprecated only for canonical replacement when two answers cannot both be true for the same context; require at least one of supersedes, superseded_by so the graph is explicit. Deprecation does not mean “old”; it means replaced default for a named scope.
  4. Optional: use see_also / related for complementary (non-conflicting) views.

docs.title: 4.5 Adopting this repository as a team template
docs.text:
Any team may use this project as a starting layout and requirements spec for their own knowledge base:

  1. Clone (or use “Use this template” on the host, or fork) into a workspace you control.
  2. Create a new empty repository on your git host (your org’s naming, visibility, and branch rules).
  3. Point origin at that new repo and push your initial branch (e.g. main), or add it as origin and push after replacing remotes—whichever matches your host’s workflow.
  4. Customize for your team: knowledge/ structure, §6 front matter, meta/ (golden queries, policies), CI, and optional Cursor skills under .cursor/skills/—the contract stays git + markdown + PR merges + local RAG (§5, §12).

Teams do not need to stay tied to an upstream “template” repo unless they want occasional merges from it; most adopters will treat their copy as the source of truth.

docs.title: 4.6 Multi-team usage, corpus growth, and development workflow
docs.text:
Multi-team / LoB model: The reusable engine (this repository’s tooling and conventions) is not the same as any one team’s corpus. Each team or LoB SHOULD maintain its own clone of the template with its own remote, so knowledge volume and governance stay owned—see §4.5. Cross-team read access is via HTTP/MCP or git dependencies, not by pushing unrelated prose into one shared knowledge tree without owners.

Branching (industry-accepted default): main is the integration line (CI-green). Contributors use short-lived feature/<slug> branches, open Pull Requests, pass required checks, then merge to main. Stable releases of the engine are tagged (e.g. v0.5.0); adopters MAY pin those tags. Long-lived parallel stable branches are discouraged unless the team documents release trains (e.g. release/0.5 patch lines).

Maintenance mechanics (normative for this repo):

  1. CONTRIBUTING.md documents merge criteria, naming, and merge-vs-new guidance.
  2. Optional CODEOWNERS enforces review for paths such as knowledge/functional/**.
  3. CI runs front matter validation, tests, golden queries, and optional index dry-run as configured.
  4. Auto-promote on main: When a PR merges to main, a GitHub Action may update touched knowledge/**/*.md files that still have status: draft to status: reviewed and set last_reviewed to the merge day (UTC). Authors can leave draft at PR time; human review stays on the PR; the promotion step is mechanical and does not replace review. Set another status (e.g. legacy_reviewed, deprecated) before merge if the doc should not be promoted this way.
  5. ki contribute (dry-run) implements retrieval-first duplicate detection (§5.8): contributors run it before opening a PR or call POST /v1/contribute_dry_run with draft markdown.
  6. Archive / low-priority docs: authors MAY set exclude_from_default_retrieval: true on low-value or historical overflow so default retrieval stays tight; callers MAY pass include_archived: true on /v1/retrieve and /v1/context_pack to include them.
  7. Opt-in git hook: scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit-validate-knowledge.sh may be installed via scripts/install-git-hooks.sh to validate staged knowledge/**/*.md locally.

docs.title: 5. RAG architecture: ingest, index, retrieve, and (optional) generate
docs.text: The whole project is organised around a RAG pipeline running locally (or in CI for validation). Authoring stays file-based and git-friendly; the RAG layer is the runtime that makes that content agent-ready.

docs.title: 5.1 Pipeline (required behaviour)
docs.text:
1. Ingest: Scan configured paths (e.g. knowledge/**/*.md).
  2. Normalize: Parse front matter; strip or preserve structure consistently.
  3. Chunk: Split into retrieval units (by heading, size, or hybrid rules), each with stable ids.
  4. Embed: Vector embeddings per chunk (model configurable; see open decisions).
  5. Store: Vector store plus optional sparse / full-text index for hybrid retrieval (recommended for exact terms and code-like tokens).
  6. Serve: Local API and/or CLI: retrieve top‑N candidates (hybrid when configured), mandatorily rerank (§5.5), then assemble context packs for agents.

On git pull or post-merge, contributors should be able to refresh the index in one step (or watch mode in dev).

docs.title: 5.2 Run locally
docs.text:
After clone, a local tool (CLI and/or API):

  1. Builds or updates the RAG index from the working tree (or pinned commit).
  2. Exposes retrieval: semantic search, hybrid search, context bundle export, health (commit, embedding model id, index schema version).

docs.title: 5.3 Index characteristics
docs.text:
• Reproducible: Same commit SHA + same chunking/embedding config → same index (or explicitly versioned deltas).
  • Performant: Incremental rebuild when files change; suitable for frequent use during development.
  • Portable: Runs on macOS/Linux (Windows optional); no mandatory cloud for daily dev (local embeddings preferred if policy requires air‑gap).

docs.title: 5.4 Smart chunking (retrieval quality)
docs.text:
“Smart” RAG here means chunks that match how people query and how prose is structured—not arbitrary fixed windows. Requirements and recommendations:

Concern Approach Boundaries Structure-aware splitting: walk the Markdown AST; primary boundaries are headings (##, ###). A section under one heading is usually one conceptual unit. Oversized sections If a heading block exceeds a max token length, sub-split by paragraph or list item, keeping overlap only on sub-splits so boundary sentences stay discoverable. Default overlap (tune in meta/): ~64–128 tokens when max chunk ≈ 512 tokens (~12–25%); ~32–64 tokens when max ≈ 256; if chunking by character length, ~10–15% overlap of the window. Heading-only chunks (whole section under one heading, under max size): 0 overlap between sections. Undersized sections Merge tiny adjacent siblings (e.g. single-line ####) up to a min size so the vector is not noise-dominated—unless they are glossary entries (keep one entry per chunk). Code and tables Code blocks and tables are often quoted verbatim in questions: either attach them as separate chunks with type: code \| table metadata, or keep them inside the parent section chunk but ensure the surrounding heading is in the same chunk for context. Front matter Strip from body chunks but store as document-level metadata replicated on every chunk from that file (filtering, faceting: area, domain, tags). Stable identities Each chunk has a deterministic chunk id (e.g. hash of file_path + heading_path + chunk_index) so incremental reindex can replace embeddings for changed chunks only.

Advanced patterns (optional, improves precision/recall):

  • Hierarchical / parent–child: Embed small child chunks for precise retrieval; at query time expand with the parent section (or preceding heading) for context in the context pack—without inflating the whole document.
  • Hypothetical questions (HyDE) or title expansion: Optional second-stage; only if validated—not required for v1.

Anti-patterns to avoid: splitting mid-sentence arbitrarily; huge chunks that dilute the embedding; tiny chunks with no semantic mass (unless glossary).

docs.title: 5.5 Smart index construction (retrieval + maintenance)
docs.text:
The index is “smart” when recall (find the right passage) and precision (little junk) are both high, and when updates are cheap.

Layer Role Dense vectors Semantic similarity: “how do we handle timeouts in service X?” matches prose that never uses the exact phrase. Sparse / full-text (BM25 or equivalent) Exact and rare tokens: API names, error codes, file paths, CLI flags, env vars. Hybrid retrieval (merge dense + sparse scores, e.g. RRF or weighted sum) is recommended for a technical KB. Metadata filters Narrow by domain, area, type from front matter before or after vector search to avoid cross-domain collisions. Reranking (mandatory) After first-stage retrieval, always run a cross-encoder or lightweight local reranker on the candidate set (e.g. retrieve 20–40 → rerank → take top 8–12 for context pack assembly). This stage is required so downstream coding assistants get optimal chunk order for analysis—not only embedding similarity. Run locally (no mandatory cloud call); if policy blocks certain models, ship an approved small reranker documented in meta/.

Mandatory reranking (normative):

  • Default pipeline: retrieve candidate_k (config default e.g. 24) → rerank with query–passage scoring → context_pack_k (e.g. 8) before §5.10 diversification rules.
  • Persist reranker model id + version next to embedding model in the index manifest for reproducibility.
  • API: responses include rerank_score (or final rank position) per chunk where applicable; health may expose reranker id.

Operational requirements:

  • Versioning: Persist embedding model name + version, chunking config hash, and index schema version with each build so behaviour is reproducible and debuggable.
  • Incremental rebuild: On change, only re-chunk and re-embed files that differ (content hash per file); unchanged files skip embedding work.
  • Evaluation (lightweight): Maintain a small golden query set in meta/ (10–30 real questions + expected file paths or heading titles). On index or chunking changes, report hit rate @k in CI or a manual script—stops regressions from “tuning” blindly.

docs.title: 5.6 “Agentic” API (behavioural requirements)
docs.text:
The API should be easy for agents and scripts to use:

  • Clear operations: retrieve (query → ranked chunks), get chunk by id, context pack (query + max tokens + min score + optional assembly profile—see §5.10), neighbours (optional graph from related: links), health (index status, corpus fingerprint—§12.1).
  • Structured responses (JSON): chunk text, file path, line range (or offsets), retrieval score, rerank score (after §5.5 mandatory rerank), embedding / reranker / index version ids; context packs include why included (e.g. hit, related, same_area, parent_section) per §5.10.
  • Metadata: repo commit, index build id, schema version; health returns index_status (missing | building | ready | stale) and sync_status (e.g. ok | blocked_dirty_tree | blocked_diverged | syncing) per §12.1–§12.2.
  • Optional: streaming assistant answers only when every factual claim can be tied to retrieved chunk ids (see §5.7).

docs.title: 5.7 Minimising hallucination in a RAG-first system
docs.text:
RAG does not guarantee truth; it guarantees grounded retrieval. Requirements:

Principle Requirement Grounding Default path for agents: retrieved chunks + citations (path + lines). Generation If the tool generates prose (summaries, answers), output must include chunk citations for claims grounded in the corpus; unsupported claims must be absent or explicitly marked as not in knowledge base. Staleness Each chunk carries source commit / mtime so UIs can warn when context predates a change. Gaps Return empty or low-confidence results clearly; no filler from model memory.

Release alignment: See §10 Product phases. MVP ships ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → mandatory rerank with mandatory citations on any synthesized answer path; retrieval-only endpoints remain the safest default for strict audits. Later phases add hybrid retrieval hardening, contribution tooling, PR bots—see §10.

docs.title: 5.8 Agent-assisted contribution: what is new vs what already exists?
docs.text:
Coding assistants are not reliable if they guess from memory. Duplicate or contradictory docs hurt trust. Contribution flows must therefore be retrieval-first and review-backed.

Principle: “Figure out what to contribute” means compare the draft against the indexed corpus using the same RAG retrieval the team uses for reading—not an unstructured chat guess.

docs.title: Required workflow (for tools / editor rules / CLI)
docs.text:
1. Index is current. Before a contribution, the developer runs (or the tool runs) an index refresh on the latest main merge base so retrieval targets current knowledge.
  2. Retrieve first. From the developer’s draft (full text or a structured outline: topic, area, summary bullets), the agent queries the RAG API with hybrid search (semantic + keywords for APIs, paths, error codes).
  3. Present evidence. The agent shows the top‑k similar chunks with paths, line ranges, and similarity scores—never a paraphrase without citations.
  4. Classify the gap (deterministic guidance). Using retrieval scores and optional rules:
  5. Near-duplicate (very high overlap with one doc): recommend editing that file (new section or revision) instead of adding a second file.
  6. Extension (related doc exists but draft adds facts): recommend patch to existing doc + update front matter (last-reviewed, related).
  7. New doc (low overlap or new area): recommend a new path under knowledge/ per §6.
  8. Human decides. The developer (or PR reviewers) confirms merge vs new file. The agent proposes a diff; PR review remains the quality gate—not model autonomy.

docs.title: Optional tooling (recommended)
docs.text:
• Contribution endpoint or script (e.g. contribute --dry-run): accepts draft markdown, returns ranked similar chunks + suggested action (edit | merge | new) + suggested paths. Actions are recommendations; scores are transparent.
  • PR automation: For changed files, run retrieval against the rest of the repo and post a comment listing possibly related docs (similarity above a threshold) to help reviewers spot duplication.

docs.title: Limits (honesty)
docs.text:
Limit Implication Similarity is statistical Borderline cases need human judgment; tune thresholds in meta/ and revisit. Corpus gaps If retrieval returns nothing, “new doc” may still overlap unindexed text—full-text grep / list by area in front matter still helps. Contradictions Retrieval surfaces conflicts; reviewers resolve per §4.4.

Success: The agent is “smart” because it always grounds the contribute decision in retrieved chunks, not because it infers from prior chat.

docs.title: 5.9 Local hosting and multi-client integration (HTTP, MCP, agnostic)
docs.text:
The knowledge base is locally hosted by default: a small HTTP API (and/or CLI) runs on the contributor’s machine next to the repo and index, not as a mandatory cloud service. Integration is assistant-agnostic (§5.12).

Requirement Detail Binding Default bind 127.0.0.1 (or localhost) on a documented port; optional config for LAN-only bind if the team explicitly allows it (document security implications). Client workflow Any coding assistant that can invoke HTTP or MCP calls the API (or MCP tools) in a retrieve-first step: query → ranked chunks / context pack → then analysis, planning, or code changes use that grounded context with citations. Examples: Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot—not a closed list. Agentic workflows: the LLM/planning loop runs in the client; Groundline provides tools (teamkm_* over HTTP) or direct REST. Transport REST + JSON as the canonical contract (versioned paths or Accept-Version); stable enough for scripts and IDE integrations. Discovery: with ki serve, GET /openapi.yaml (source file) and GET /openapi.json (same spec as JSON). Authentication (local) MVP: no auth on loopback, or optional shared secret in config if bind is non-loopback—document in meta/. Multiple MCP servers The system SHOULD expose the same retrieval operations via an MCP server process so clients that speak MCP (e.g. Cursor with multiple MCPs enabled) can add this knowledge MCP alongside other MCPs (browser, git-host, ticketing, etc.). No requirement that this MCP is exclusive—teams run several MCP servers concurrently. Reference implementation: pip install -e ".[mcp]" then python3 -m ki mcp (stdio); tools teamkm_health, teamkm_retrieve, teamkm_context_pack, teamkm_contribute_dry_run, prompt teamkm_retrieve_first — each tool HTTP-calls the local API (TEAMKM_API_BASE or KI_HOST+KI_PORT). Coexistence Namespace MCP tool names with a project prefix (e.g. teamkm_*) to avoid collisions with tools from other MCPs on the same host.

Implementation note: MCP is a thin adapter over the HTTP API (not a second index path): start ki serve, run ki mcp as the host’s MCP subprocess; behaviour must stay consistent between transports (same query → same ranked chunks for a given index version).

docs.title: 5.10 Smart context assembly and relations (better agent outcomes)
docs.text: Raw “top‑k similar chunks” often under-serve agents: they may be redundant, miss linked docs, or omit the complementary view (e.g. QE testing notes when the query sounds technical). Groundline implements context assembly that builds coherent bundles with explicit structure so any integrated coding assistant performs better after the retrieve step. MVP (required): cap chunks per document, expand explicit related links, attach inclusion_reason per chunk, group output for readability. V1+ (recommended): MMR / diversify, cross‑domain same‑area expansion, optional intent / profile / role hints—see §10.

docs.title: 5.10.1 Relation sources (built at index time)
docs.text:
The index SHOULD derive a lightweight document graph (no need for a heavy graph DB in MVP):

Link type Source Use Explicit Front matter related: [...], inline links to other knowledge/**/*.md Always expand with at least the linked doc’s title + one chunk or abstract Hierarchical Parent heading / doc outline (## path) Expand child hit with parent section for surrounding intent Same thread Shared area + product (and optionally tags overlap) Suggest cross-domain neighbours: e.g. pull testing + functional when area matches and query is broad Supersession supersedes / superseded_by, status: deprecated Prefer canonical chunk; optionally include deprecated only with a “superseded” warning

docs.title: 5.10.2 Context pack assembly (behaviour)
docs.text:
A context pack is not a flat list: it is a budgeted set of chunks (by max tokens / max chunks) assembled with rules:

  1. Retrieve top‑N candidates (hybrid when §10 V1+ is available; else semantic-first in MVP).
  2. Rerank (mandatory, §5.5): score candidates with query–passage reranker; order by rerank_score before diversification.
  3. Diversify (MVP: required): cap chunks per document so one long note does not crowd out others. V1+ (recommended): add MMR or equivalent for extra diversity (after rerank ordering).
  4. Relational expansion: MVP: always follow front matter related: (and inline knowledge/...md links when trivially detectable). V1+: optional same-area, different-domain peers when profile: full (or similar) requests a full picture (technical + functional + testing).
  5. Ordering: group by domain or relation role in the JSON (so clients can prompt “Engineering”, “Product”, “QA”)—recommended in MVP, required in V1+ for multi-domain packs.
  6. Budget: fill up to max_tokens with declining priority: direct hits → explicit links → optional cross-domain fillers.
  7. Transparency (MVP: required): each chunk lists inclusion_reason: hit \| expanded_parent \| related_doc \| same_area_peer \| deprecated_warning.

docs.title: 5.10.3 Optional hints (improve relevance)
docs.text:
• intent or profile query params (e.g. coding, testing, product, mixed): nudge metadata filters and relation weights—not required for MVP but recommended for V1+.
  • role hint (dev | qe | pm): slight boost to matching author_role / domain—optional.

docs.title: 5.10.4 Why this improves downstream agent analysis
docs.text:
• Mandatory reranking (§5.5) fixes ordering where embedding similarity alone is misleading—so the best passages lead the context pack.
  • Relations supply missing halves of the story (implementation + acceptance + how we test).
  • Diversity reduces duplicate context that wastes the context window.
  • Structured grouping matches how multi-step analysis works in agent tools.
  • Citations + inclusion_reason keep outputs auditable (§5.7).

docs.title: 5.11 Advanced RAG implementation ladder (beyond naïve embed → cosine top‑k)
docs.text: “Smart” RAG here is layered: several specialised stages, each fixing a different failure mode of naïve embed → cosine top‑k. The normative minimum for this product is already in §5.4–§5.7, §5.10, and §10; this subsection ties optional / V1+ advances into one ladder.

docs.title: 5.11.1 Retrieval stack (precision + recall)
docs.text: Layer What it fixes Notes Hybrid retrieval Exact tokens (paths, APIs, errors) vs fuzzy meaning Dense + BM25 / sparse; fuse (e.g. RRF or weighted sum)—V1+ hardening (§10). Query side Vague or mismatched wording Optional (measure first): light query rewrite or HyDE only where a golden set shows lift—otherwise skip (latency + risk). Mandatory rerank Wrong ordering in top‑k Normative (§5.5): cross‑encoder or lightweight local reranker on 20–40 → 8–12 (typical). MMR / caps per doc One doc dominating the window After rerank: diversify—MVP caps per doc; V1+ optional MMR (§5.10).

docs.title: 5.11.2 Context assembly (what goes to the assistant)
docs.text:
Many simple RAG systems stop too early; Groundline does not (§5.10):

Technique Role Graph‑light expansion related, same area / product, parent heading—deterministic rules + token budget, not a giant graph DB on day one. Multi‑granularity Small chunks for retrieval; optional parent window for generation (retrieve child → expand to section). V1+ recommended where measured. Structured packs Group by domain (technical / functional / testing) so downstream models attend consistently.

docs.title: 5.11.3 Smarter than one‑shot retrieve (optional)
docs.text: Pattern Use Decomposed queries Complex question → 2–3 sub‑queries → merge/dedup → one rerank pass. Iterative / agentic retrieval First pass narrows area/doc set; second drills into linked docs—only with logged steps, capped iterations, and citations per claim (§5.7).

docs.title: 5.11.4 Operations that improve quality over time
docs.text:
• Golden query set + recall@k / nDCG after rerank—tune chunking, hybrid weights, reranker from data (§5.5, §7, §11).
  • Offline reprocessing when embedding or reranker model changes—version in manifest (§5.5, §12).
  • Stale / conflict handling (deprecated, supersedes) so retrieval does not blend contradictions silently (§4.4, §5.10).

docs.title: 5.11.5 Anti‑patterns (often look “advanced” but hurt)
docs.text:
Avoid Why Huge chunks “for more context” Dilutes embeddings; hurts retrieval precision. Heavy HyDE on every query without eval Adds latency and hallucination surface. End‑to‑end LLM chooses what to retrieve with no citation lock Hard to trust in a KB product; conflicts with §5.7.

Summary ladder (aligned with this spec): hybrid retrieve (V1+) → mandatory rerank (MVP) → graph‑light / relational context pack (MVP) → citation‑locked downstream use (§5.7). Add query rewrite, multi‑hop, or iterative retrieval only when the golden set proves they help.

docs.title: 5.12 Coding-assistant agnosticism (cross–agent coding assistant)
docs.text:
Groundline MUST NOT depend on a single vendor IDE or model. The product contract is:

Layer Role Assistant binding Canonical REST + JSON (versioned) on localhost None — any client can curl, script, or use a generated SDK. Optional MCP stdio server (python3 -m ki mcp) exposing the same operations as tools that call the REST API None — any host that loads MCP can attach; optional [mcp] install. Optional CLI (retrieve, context-pack, health) None — terminal-only workflows. Optional UX .cursor/skills/*, editor-specific hooks Cursor (or similar)—convenience only; not required to use the knowledge base.

Requirements:

  1. No proprietary-only APIs as the only integration path—HTTP remains documented and stable.
  2. Naming: user-facing docs and examples MUST list multiple assistants where relevant (“Cursor, Claude Code, …”) and state that others work via the same REST/MCP surfaces.
  3. Session / trigger language: §12.1 uses “coding assistant session” as the abstract trigger; one team’s recipe (e.g. Claude in terminal + MCP) is an example, not an exclusive platform lock.
  4. OpenAPI: ship docs/openapi.yaml in-repo; ki serve exposes GET /openapi.yaml and GET /openapi.json for clients and code generators.
  5. Testing: golden queries and health checks run against HTTP (or CLI)—not against a single IDE plugin.

Anti-patterns: hard-coding only the Cursor SDK; requiring a single model provider for retrieval (embedding/rerank are local/configurable, not “Claude-only”).

docs.title: 6. Information architecture (repository layout — draft)
docs.text:
Suggested top-level structure (adjust in review):

knowledge/
  technical/
    architecture/
    runbooks/
    decisions/          # ADR-style
  delivery/             # Completed work, analysis, discussion summaries (organise by component, feature area, or time period — team picks convention)
  testing/              # QE-led: test plans, regression notes, quality findings
  functional/
    glossary/
    features/
  meta/                 # how to contribute, templates, golden queries, evaluated SLOs
.templates/             # doc templates (optional)
scripts/                # RAG indexer, embedding pipeline, local API server

docs.title: 6.1 Front matter schema (YAML)
docs.text:
Every knowledge/**/*.md file MUST include YAML front matter between --- lines. CI validates required keys by path (see table).

Key Required when Type Purpose title Always string Human title for lists and UI domain Always (see Domain inference below) string technical | delivery | testing | functional | meta — RAG metadata filters; canonical value is determined by file path under knowledge/ area Always string Product or system area (e.g. billing, auth, reports) — links dev, QE, PM, DM to the same feature/product surface tags Optional string[] Fine-grained labels author_role Always string dev | qe | pm | dm | mixed type Always string Doc kind: e.g. adr, runbook, delivery-summary, test-plan, feature, glossary status Always string draft | reviewed | legacy_reviewed | deprecated last_reviewed When status: reviewed or legacy_reviewed ISO date YYYY-MM-DD Freshness and staleness warnings canonical_since Optional when legacy_reviewed ISO date YYYY-MM-DD When this doc became non-default / historical for the current product line (still valid under applies_to) applies_to Optional string[] Version/scope tags (e.g. product:acme:v1, stack:jdk8, env:prod-eu) for retrieval filtering and legacy-friendly truth doc_version Optional string Document or bundle version for humans and filters (e.g. v2.1) exclude_from_default_retrieval Optional boolean If true, omit from default /v1/retrieve and /v1/context_pack unless caller passes include_archived: true (use for archive overflow or low-signal notes) product Recommended under functional/** string Product or offering the note supports (helps PM/DM queries) related Optional string[] Paths to other .md files in this repo supersedes / superseded_by When status: deprecated (at least one required) string Replacement graph for conflicting defaults only (§4.4) contributor Optional string Display name of the person who last substantively edited the note—often pre-filled from local author profile (§6.2) team Optional string Squad or team name—pre-filled from profile when helpful for DM/PM filters topics_author Optional string[] Topics this author focuses on (may overlap tags)—from profile; helps retrieval when filtering “who knows what”

Path norms:

  • knowledge/functional/** → domain: functional; author_role often pm or mixed.
  • knowledge/testing/** → domain: testing; author_role often qe.
  • knowledge/delivery/** → domain: delivery; author_role often dev.
  • knowledge/technical/** → domain: technical; author_role often dev.
  • knowledge/meta/** (if used for indexed meta docs) → domain: meta.

Domain inference (canonical):

  1. The first path segment after knowledge/ MUST be one of: technical, delivery, testing, functional, meta. That segment is the canonical domain for the file.
  2. If front matter includes domain, it MUST equal the canonical value from the path; otherwise CI fails the PR (stops silent drift between path and metadata).
  3. Authors MAY omit domain while editing; before merge, scripts/validate_frontmatter.py (or equivalent) MUST inject domain from the path or fail the PR if it is missing and injection is not enabled—teams choose one policy; the default SHOULD be inject so agents only need to place the file under the right subtree.
  4. Optional later: a --fix (or write) mode on the validator writes the correct domain into the file locally so contributors run one command before git add.

Validation: PR CI runs a schema + path/domain check; invalid front matter fails the PR. Optional keys (contributor, team, topics_author) SHOULD be allowed by the schema when present.

docs.title: 6.2 Local author profile (optional editor skill, not committed)
docs.text:
So each member does not re-type name, team, topics, the repo MAY ship an editor skill for Cursor (.cursor/skills/knowledge-author-profile/)—convenience only (§5.12)—that tells the agent to read a local YAML profile:

  • Canonical path: meta/author-profile.local.yaml (gitignored).
  • Example template: meta/author-profile.example.yaml (committed).
  • Machine-wide optional: ~/.teamkm/profile.yaml — project-local file wins when present.

The agent uses the profile to suggest §6.1 fields when committing knowledge (author_role, tags, area, optional contributor, team, topics_author). Humans still approve PR content; profile data never forces incorrect area on a doc.

docs.title: 7. Non-functional requirements
docs.text:
Corpus assumptions (adjust in meta/): on the order of 10²–10³ files and ~10–50 MB raw markdown—large enough that incremental index updates matter.

Area Requirement (draft SLOs — tighten as the corpus grows) Full index build On a typical developer laptop, full rebuild stays under ~15 minutes at MVP; stretch under ~5 minutes with a mature incremental pipeline. Incremental build After a small change, p95 rebuild dominated by re-embed of touched files, target under ~2 minutes (document actuals in meta/). Retrieve / context pack API p95 latency under ~500 ms per query locally, excluding cold start (cold start allowed if documented once). Retrieval quality Golden query set (§5.5): recall@5 (correct doc in top 5) ≥ 80% before changing default chunking without sign-off (threshold evolves with the eval set). Scale Document behaviour at 2× and 5× reference corpus size (capacity planning). Security No secrets in repo; pre-merge secret-pattern checks; air‑gap: no calls to unapproved embedding endpoints. Observability Log index duration, files changed, chunk/embed counts, errors; optional p95 API latency. Licensing Document embedding model + vector store license in meta/.

docs.title: 8. CI/CD (recommended)
docs.text:
• On PR: markdown lint, broken-link check, front matter schema (§6.1), optional golden-query regression on dry-run index.
  • Dry-run RAG index build in CI (or validate chunk counts + schema) so broken content fails before merge.
  • On merge to default branch: optional versioned index artefact (§12)—not required if all consumers build locally.

docs.title: 9. Open decisions (to fill in as you progress)
docs.text:
• [ ] PR policy: minimum reviewers, CODEOWNERS per path.
  • [ ] RAG tooling stack: vector store (e.g. Chroma, LanceDB, Qdrant local); optional hybrid sparse index (SQLite FTS, Tantivy, etc.).
  • [ ] Embedding model: local vs API; dimension; offline / air-gap requirement; same model pinned in CI for reproducibility.
  • [ ] Reranker model: cross-encoder vs lightweight ranker; approved local model list; candidate_k / context_pack_k defaults.
  • [ ] Chunking strategy: max tokens per chunk; sub-split defaults; overlap values (starting defaults in §5.4).
  • [ ] API surface: default port, loopback-only defaults; REST contract versioning; MCP tool naming is teamkm_* in the reference server (ki mcp); teams MAY alias in host config.
  • [ ] Multiple MCPs: document how many concurrent MCP connections the team uses and example configs for major hosts (Cursor, Claude Code, …) plus generic JSON—no single-vendor lock-in.
  • [ ] Retention: how to deprecate or archive stale docs.
  • [ ] Naming/versioning of the repo and index schema.
  • [ ] Delivery doc granularity: one doc per small change vs one living doc per feature area; filename and folder convention.
  • [ ] Contribution thresholds: similarity cutoffs for "edit existing" vs "new doc"; whether PR bot posts related-doc hints.
  • [ ] External refs: keep zero ticket linkage vs optional opaque internal ids (see §3—do not block MVP).
  • [ ] Numeric SLOs: replace §7 placeholders with measured p95 after first production-sized corpus.
  • [ ] Auto-index: core.hooksPath vs per-repo .git/hooks; fingerprint strategy (git HEAD vs content hash); lockfile location.
  • [ ] Auto-sync: poll interval; ff-only vs merge strategy; behaviour when dirty/diverged; opt-out for active contributors.
  • [ ] Terminal session hook: MCP loaded by the assistant vs scripts/ki-session.sh wrapper vs shell cd hook; which one the team standardizes on.

docs.title: 10. Product phases (MVP and later)
docs.text: Phase Goal In scope MVP Compound knowledge from PRs and make it retrievable Markdown under knowledge/; ingest → structure-aware chunk → embed → vector store; mandatory local rerank after first-stage retrieve (§5.5); locally hosted HTTP API on loopback (§5.9) so any assistant can call retrieve/context_pack; assistant-agnostic integration (§5.12); primary trigger: coding-assistant session starts MCP/API (§12.1) → auto-sync + auto-index when safe/stale; health with index_status and sync_status; context packs with per-doc caps, related: expansion, inclusion_reason (§5.10); optional MCP server exposing the same ops; citations on all passages; front matter §6.1 + CI validation; author profile skill + local yaml (§6.2, optional); golden query file in meta/ (manual or CI). V1+ Better recall/precision and smarter context Hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse/BM25); MMR / richer diversification; optional cross-domain same-area expansion and intent/profile hints (§5.10); incremental pipeline hardened; optional contribute --dry-run (§5.8); MCP tool set hardened for multi-MCP Cursor setups. V2 Operational excellence Optional PR bot (related docs); optional published index artefacts for shared consumers (§12).

docs.title: 11. Success metrics and adoption
docs.text: Metric Meaning Starting target Corpus growth Markdown files + merged PRs to knowledge/ per month Non-zero steady growth; DM/PM review trends in standups Golden-set recall@k Correct relevant doc in top k ≥ 80% @5 before changing defaults (§7) Index build SLO Full + incremental times Meet §7 until corpus outgrows—then re-benchmark Role coverage At least one reviewed doc per domain (technical, delivery, testing, functional) per major area / product Expands as products/features evolve Adoption (qualitative) Dev/QE/PM/DM report using context packs for new and existing feature work Periodic survey or retro note

docs.title: 12. Operations: who builds the index and where it lives
docs.text:
• Source of truth is always git: every merged PR adds to the corpus; knowledge compounds with each merge.
  • Default (MVP): each contributor (or local automation) runs index build after pull or merge; generated index files live under a gitignored path (e.g. .rag/index/) documented in the repo README—not committed unless the team explicitly chooses artefact storage.
  • Serving: Start the local API (and optionally MCP) after the index is built; coding assistants connect to localhost (§5.9) to retrieve before analyze—no separate cloud dependency for that path.
  • CI: validates corpus + schema + optional dry-run build; may emit non-committed logs or metrics.
  • Optional (V2): publish a versioned index tarball per main SHA for teams that want identical local behaviour without rebuilding (still derived from the same commit).

docs.title: 12.1 Automatic indexing on checkout and on coding-assistant session start
docs.text:
Goal: when a team member checks out this repo (clone, checkout, pull) or starts a coding-assistant session (terminal or IDE) with this project, indexing begins without a manual step so retrieval is warm or warming. Details are assistant-agnostic (§5.12).

Primary hook (MVP): assistant session starts MCP or local API. The team picks one documented entrypoint. Groundline MUST tie indexing (and optional upstream sync—§12.2) to that moment:

Trigger Required behaviour (MVP) Coding-assistant session (primary) At least one pattern MUST be documented and supported: (A) MCP: the host assistant loads Groundline MCP so initialize runs the local API or attached service → background sync (§12.2, if enabled) → background index if missing/stale (works for any MCP-capable assistant). (B) Shell wrapper (e.g. scripts/ki-session.sh) that the team aliases to their assistant CLI (claude, cursor, etc.), which spawns API/MCP then execs the real binary (non-blocking fork where possible). (C) direnv / .envrc or shell function that runs ki ensure-index & when cwd is this repo (weaker: per-shell, not per assistant invocation). (A) or (B) is preferred. Fresh clone / checkout / pull Optional (supplementary): git hooks (e.g. post-checkout, post-merge) or ./scripts/install-hooks.sh. On trigger, run index build in the background if missing or stale. Opt-in install—see caveat below. Hooks do not replace the session path. MCP / local API initialize Whenever the MCP server or local API starts: (1) /health with index_status, sync_status (§12.2), corpus_fingerprint, optional progress; (2) enqueue background sync (if enabled) then index if missing/stale; (3) do not block handshake on full completion—degraded retrieval until ready (§5.9). IDE workspace open Recommended (V1+): editor “on folder open” or hooks—same non-blocking rules; secondary to MCP for portability across assistants.

Staleness / fingerprint: persist a small file under .rag/ (gitignored), e.g. .rag/manifest.json: corpus_fingerprint (hash of sorted (relpath, sha256 content) for knowledge/** or git tree HEAD + chunking config hash + embedding model id). If fingerprint mismatch → stale → rebuild (incremental when implemented).

Concurrency: use a single-flight lock (e.g. .rag/build.lock or OS lock) so overlapping triggers (pull + MCP start) do not run parallel full embeds.

User experience: README states: “First use may build the index in the background; wait until GET /health shows ready or watch logs.” Optionally a desktop notice is out of scope for MVP.

Important caveat (Git hooks): Git does not run server-side hooks on git clone. Client hooks run only after local git actions and only if installed. “Index on clone, zero steps” is not guaranteed by hooks alone. Primary path for teams: an assistant session starts MCP/API (§12.1 first row)—runs without git hook install. True “on clone with zero install” still needs the user to open a session (or configure MCP) at least once—document in README.

docs.title: 12.2 Automatic sync with upstream (no manual git pull for consumers)
docs.text:
Goal: when new commits land on the tracked upstream branch (e.g. origin/main), local clones update automatically so the knowledge corpus and index track the latest merged PRs without the user running git pull manually.

Safety (non-negotiable): automation must not clobber work. Default rules:

Condition Behaviour Clean working tree and index; local branch can fast-forward Run git fetch then git merge --ff-only (or equivalent git pull --ff-only) to the configured upstream. No rebase, no force. Dirty working tree (uncommitted changes) Do not pull. Surface sync_status: blocked_dirty_tree via health (§5.6) and logs; optionally notify once. User resolves or commits. Diverged (local commits not on upstream, non-FF) Do not auto-merge. Surface sync_status: blocked_diverged; user must integrate manually (branch, rebase, or merge as per team policy). Detached HEAD or no upstream Do not pull unless Groundline.sync.upstream is explicitly set; surface sync_status: not_configured.

Triggers (MVP—at least one must be implemented; all may coexist):

  1. Same as indexing—assistant session: on MCP initialize (when the coding assistant loads MCP), run fetch + ff-only (§12.2 rules) then reindex if HEAD changed—primary alignment with “start session = up to date when safe.”
  2. Periodic timer inside MCP/API: e.g. every 5–30 min (default 15 min) for clones where the session stays open—catches upstream pushes without restarting the assistant.
  3. Optional daemon: documented teamkm sync long-running command that only fetch/ff-only + reindex.
  4. Git hooks supplement only; not sufficient when others push upstream unless combined with (1) or (2).

Configuration (documented env or config file):

  • upstream_remote (default origin), upstream_branch (default main or tracked branch).
  • sync_interval_seconds (0 = only on MCP start, no periodic poll).
  • sync_enabled (default true for “read-only” clones; false for contributors actively committing—recommended default true with dirty-tree blocking).

Transparency: /health (or MCP tool) SHOULD include sync_status, last_sync_at, local_head, upstream_head (after fetch) so any integrated assistant can report “knowledge is current as of …” or “sync blocked—uncommitted changes”.

Relationship to indexing: after a successful ff-only merge, corpus fingerprint changes → §12.1 marks index stale and background rebuild runs (same lock as index build).

docs.title: 13. Success criteria (first milestone)
docs.text:
1. Repository exists with governance (PR-only to main) and documented contribution rules.
  2. Developers can clone the repo; starting a coding-assistant session (per §12.1 primary path) triggers background upstream sync (if enabled, §12.2) and index build when missing/stale; optional git hooks remain supplementary. A manual one-command full build remains available.
  3. Locally hosted API (or CLI) on loopback supports retrieval with mandatory reranking (§5.5) and cited chunks (path + line range + text, retrieval + rerank scores); any generated answer path attaches citations per §5.7. Documented integration for HTTP and MCP so any supported assistant can call before analysis (§5.9, §5.12). /health exposes sync_status and index_status (§12.1, §12.2).
  4. At least one technical, one delivery, one testing (QE), and one functional example—each with valid §6.1 front matter—so dev, QE, PM, and DM can retrieve cross-role context for a shared area / product.
  5. A second merged PR in the same area proves compounding: retrieval returns both older and newer chunks so feature work and maintenance benefit from prior contributions.
  6. A contribute path (rule, script, or API) demonstrates retrieve → compare → suggest edit vs new file with cited similar chunks.

docs.title: Testing and safety guardrails (Groundline)
docs.text:
This document describes how we test the repo today and how we avoid corrupting knowledge, local index state, or git history as we add the RAG stack.

Normative requirements remain in REQUIREMENTS.md (§8 CI, §7 SLOs). Architecture is in ARCHITECTURE.md.

docs.title: 1. What we test today
docs.text:
Layer Purpose Command Front matter Schema + path/domain rules (§6.1) python3 scripts/validate_frontmatter.py Index + API Chunk → index → hybrid retrieve (dense+BM25, RRF) → rerank → context_pack; /v1/health; /openapi.json pytest (includes tests/test_index.py, tests/test_api.py, tests/test_hybrid.py, tests/test_golden_eval.py) Index freshness Corpus fingerprint vs manifest; index_stale on /v1/health python3 -m ki --root . status or pytest tests/test_index_status.py MCP (optional) Stdio server python3 -m ki --root . mcp calls the HTTP API; install pip install -e ".[mcp]" Manual: configure host + run python3 -m ki --root . serve; no pytest cover of full MCP handshake yet Golden queries recall@k + mean MRR@k vs meta/golden_queries.yaml python3 scripts/golden_queries.py --root . or python3 -m ki --root . eval --report md Contribute dry-run Merge-vs-new hints from retrieval (§5.8) python3 -m ki --root . contribute -f draft.md Unit tests Validator, atomic writes pytest (after pip install -e ".[dev]")

Optional:

  • python3 scripts/validate_frontmatter.py --inject-domain — CI default may require explicit domain in files; use this where teams omit domain and inject at commit time.

docs.title: 2.1 Corpus (git)
docs.text:
• Source of truth is Markdown in knowledge/ under version control — never auto-edit without an explicit --fix (validate_frontmatter.py).
  • Atomic writes — --fix uses a temp file in the same directory + os.replace() so a crash mid-write cannot leave a half-written .md (ki/atomicio.py).
  • Validation before write — --fix only rewrites after all other required checks pass; otherwise it prints errors and skips the file.
  • Domain lock — domain must match the first folder under knowledge/ unless --inject-domain / --fix is used (§6.1 Domain inference).

docs.title: 2.2 Generated index (.rag/)
docs.text:
Implemented patterns (MVP):

  • index/ payload — chunks.json, idf.json, vectors.json written as normal files (atomizing each file write is a future tighten-up).
  • manifest.json — updated with corpus_fingerprint, index_status, model ids, chunk_count, built via atomic write (ki/manifest.py).
  • Single-flight lock — .rag/build.lock with fcntl flock where available (ki/lockfile.py).
  • Staleness — if corpus_fingerprint ≠ live hash of knowledge/**/*.md, python3 -m ki --root . index / ensure_index() rebuilds; python3 -m ki --root . status and GET /v1/health expose index_stale (§12.1).

docs.title: 2.3 Git operations (future auto-sync)
docs.text: • Never auto-merge when dirty or diverged; only fetch + fast-forward when safe (§12.2). Surface sync_status on /health when the API exists.

docs.title: 3. Recovery
docs.text: Failure Recovery Bad front matter in a PR CI fails; fix YAML locally; re-run validate_frontmatter.py. --fix interrupted Atomic rename either completes or old file remains; no half file. Re-run --fix. Corrupt .rag/ (future) Delete .rag/ (gitignored) and rebuild from current HEAD; manifest rebuild restores consistency. Wrong domain in file Run python3 scripts/validate_frontmatter.py --fix knowledge/... to set from path.

docs.title: 4. CI (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
Workflow ci.yml runs:

  1. Install Python 3.11
  2. pip install -e ".[dev,mcp]" — mcp extra so imports of ki/mcp_server.py stay compatible with packaging
  3. pytest
  4. python3 scripts/validate_frontmatter.py --root "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
  5. python3 scripts/golden_queries.py --root "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"

docs.title: 5. Optional local pre-commit
docs.text:
./scripts/install-git-hooks.sh

Validates staged knowledge/**/*.md with validate_frontmatter.py.

docs.title: 6. Future tests (RAG pipeline)
docs.text:
When ingest/index code lands, add:

  • Golden-query regression (REQUIREMENTS §5.5, §11): small fixed query set → expected doc paths.
  • Indexer idempotence: two builds from the same tree → same manifest hash.
  • Concurrent build: second process should block or no-op (single-flight).

docs.title: Contributing to Groundline
docs.text: This repo is a reusable template: Markdown corpus under knowledge/, a local index under .rag/ (gitignored), and git + PRs for governance. Normative behaviour is in docs/REQUIREMENTS.md.

docs.title: Branch workflow (default)
docs.text:
• main: integration branch; should stay CI-green (pytest + golden queries + front matter).
  • feature/<short-slug>: branch from main, open a Pull Request, delete after merge.
  • Releases: tag the engine (e.g. v0.6.0) when you want downstream teams to pin a known-good template.

GitHub main protection: enable in the repo Settings → Branches (required PR + required check test). Private repos on some plans may need Pro for full API/UI protection—see docs/GITHUB_BRANCH_PROTECTION.md.

Draft → reviewed on main (automated): After merge to main, CI may run scripts/promote_draft_on_merge.py for touched knowledge files and promote status: draft to reviewed, setting last_reviewed (UTC date). You still get human review on the PR; you do not need to edit YAML by hand for that step. Use legacy_reviewed, deprecated, or another non-draft status before merge if the file should not be auto-promoted.

docs.title: Before you open a PR
docs.text:
1. Validate front matter — python3 scripts/validate_frontmatter.py --root . (use --inject-domain if your team omits domain in drafts).
  2. Retrieval-first contribute (recommended) — see §5.8: 
    python3 -m ki --root . contribute -f path/to/draft.md
    or pipe markdown on stdin. Prefer edit or extend when similarity is high.
  3. Run tests — pytest.
  4. Index freshness (if you changed knowledge/) — python3 -m ki --root . status then python3 -m ki --root . index when stale.
  5. Golden queries — python3 scripts/golden_queries.py --root . or python3 -m ki --root . eval --report md (recall@k + MRR; see docs/TESTING.md).

docs.title: What to commit
docs.text:
• Knowledge under knowledge/<technical|delivery|testing|functional|meta>/... with §6.1 YAML front matter.
  • No raw chat logs, ticket threads, secrets, or PII (REQUIREMENTS §3).

docs.title: Corpus maintenance (avoid unbounded growth)
docs.text:
• Prefer one living doc per area plus short delivery notes that link into it.
  • For legacy behaviour that is still true for older lines, use status: legacy_reviewed, applies_to, and doc_version — do not delete working history (§4.4).
  • Use status: deprecated only when two “current” answers conflict for the same scope; set supersedes / superseded_by.
  • For low-signal overflow, use exclude_from_default_retrieval: true; retrieval APIs accept include_archived: true when needed.

docs.title: Optional: local pre-commit hook
docs.text:
./scripts/install-git-hooks.sh

Validates staged knowledge/**/*.md with validate_frontmatter.py.

docs.title: Optional: MCP (assistant hosts)
docs.text:
The local HTTP API is the canonical surface. For IDEs that speak MCP, install pip install -e ".[mcp]", run python3 -m ki --root . serve (default http://127.0.0.1:8765), then python3 -m ki --root . mcp as the MCP server command. The host runs the agent loop; tools teamkm_* call health / retrieve / context_pack / contribute_dry_run. Policy: retrieve before editing code or adding knowledge; use teamkm_contribute_dry_run before opening new docs (§5.8). Override base URL with TEAMKM_API_BASE (or KI_HOST / KI_PORT).

Full table and examples: docs/MCP.md.

docs.title: CODEOWNERS
docs.text: Edit .github/CODEOWNERS so important paths always get a reviewer.

docs.title: For engineering
docs.text: You: build, operate, and review the corpus and tooling. Success: CI-green PRs, a local index when you need grounded retrieval, optional MCP in the IDE.

docs.title: Week 1
docs.text:
1. Skim How to use Groundline and Contributing.
  2. Clone your team’s repo (after template adoption).
  3. Run the quick start below; confirm /v1/health reports index ready.
  4. Open a small knowledge/technical/ doc via PR; let merge automation set reviewed if you used draft.

docs.title: Quick start (snippets)
docs.text:
cd /path/to/your-teamkm
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"

python3 -m ki --root . index
python3 -m ki --root . serve

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/health | python3 -m json.tool

Example retrieve:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/retrieve \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"How does draft promotion work?","pack_k":5}' | python3 -m json.tool

python3 -m ki --root . serve   # in one terminal
